title: Two grandsons, two opposed images
odia:
ପୁଅର ପୁଅ ନାତି
ମାରଇ ଝିଙ୍କର କାତି
ଝିଅର ପୁଅ ନାତି
ସରଗେ ଜାଳଇ ବତୀ।
literal_meaning: The son’s son is a grandson: he strikes with the porcupine’s kati [contextually, a quill]. The daughter’s son is a grandson: he lights a lamp in heaven.
meaning_odia: ପୁଅର ପୁଅ ଓ ଝିଅର ପୁଅ—ଦୁହେଁ ନାତି, ଅଥଚ ପଙ୍କ୍ତିର ବକ୍ତା ପ୍ରଥମକୁ ଝିଙ୍କର କାତି ମାରିବା ସହ, ଦ୍ୱିତୀୟକୁ ସରଗରେ ବତୀ ଜାଳିବା ସହ ଯୋଡ଼ିଛନ୍ତି। ଏଠାରେ କାତିକୁ ପ୍ରସଙ୍ଗକ୍ରମେ ଝିଙ୍କକଣ୍ଟା ଭାବେ ପଢ଼ାଯାଇଛି; ଏହି ନିର୍ଦ୍ଦିଷ୍ଟ ଶବ୍ଦର ଅର୍ଥ ସ୍ୱତନ୍ତ୍ରଭାବେ ନିଶ୍ଚିତ ହୋଇନାହିଁ। ଆଘାତ ଓ ଆଲୋକର ଦୁଇ ଚିତ୍ରରେ ବକ୍ତାଙ୍କ ପକ୍ଷପାତ ଫୁଟିଛି; ନାତିମାନଙ୍କ ଗୁଣ ବିଷୟରେ ଏହାକୁ ସତ୍ୟ ନିୟମ ଧରାଯାଇନାହିଁ।
explanation: Both children have the same kinship name, yet the speaker gives them opposite images: a hurtful strike and a light in heaven. Read editorially, the verse favours the daughter’s son over the son’s son. That preference belongs to the speaker; the verse does not establish how either kind of grandson actually behaves.
usage_example: Original imagined example: While discussing old family sayings, a reader quotes this verse to show how the same kinship label can carry sharply unequal expectations, then questions that preference.
cultural_context: The repeated ନାତି makes the contrast especially pointed. The heavenly lamp supplies a favourable image, but the verse does not name a ceremony, recipient or religious obligation. In translation, kati is retained because its precise lexical sense remains uncertain; a porcupine quill is the contextual reading.

graphic.caption: An imagined pair of symbols preserves the speaker’s contrast without assigning it to actual children.

odia_summary: ଦୁଇ ପ୍ରକାର ନାତିକୁ ଆଘାତ ଓ ଆଲୋକର ବିପରୀତ ଚିତ୍ରରେ ଦେଖୁଥିବା ବକ୍ତା।
english_summary: A speaker contrasts two lines of grandchildren through hurt and heavenly light.
